# Probability {#sec-probability}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Code in this chapter uses **R**.
:::

Statistics draws conclusions from data that could have come out
differently. A different random sample would give a different $\bar{x}$; a
repeated experiment would give a different $\hat{p}$. To say how much to
trust a conclusion, you need a language for describing chance. That language
is **probability**, and this chapter introduces the parts of it you will use
for the rest of the book.

## Basic ideas of probability

### Random processes, outcomes, and events

A **random process** is any activity whose result can't be predicted in
advance, but which has a known set of possible results: flipping a coin,
rolling a die, choosing a student at random from a class. Each possible
result is an **outcome**, and the collection of all outcomes is the
**sample space**.

An **event** is a collection of outcomes, usually described in words. When
you roll one die, the sample space is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. The event "roll
an even number" is the collection $\{2, 4, 6\}$. We name events with capital
letters, such as $A$, and write $P(A)$ for the **probability** of $A$: a
number between 0 and 1 measuring how likely $A$ is to happen. An
**impossible event**, one that can never happen, has probability 0; a
**certain event**, one that always happens, has probability 1.

### Three ways to find a probability

**Equally likely outcomes.** When every outcome in the sample space is equally
likely, the probability of an event is a matter of counting:
$$
P(A) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{number of outcomes in the sample space}}.
$$ {#eq-classical}
For a fair die, $P(\text{even}) = 3/6 = 0.5$.

Be sure the outcomes really are equally likely before using
@eq-classical. When you roll two dice, there are 11 possible sums, from 2
to 12, but they are *not* equally likely: a sum of 7 can happen in six
ways, while a sum of 2 happens only when both dice show 1. So
$P(\text{sum is 7})$ is not $1/11$.

To use @eq-classical correctly, list outcomes that *are* equally likely.
Each die shows 1 to 6, so a roll of two dice has $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally
likely outcomes, one for each cell of @tbl-dice-sums.

| First die ↓, second die → | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|:---------:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **1**     | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | **7** |
| **2**     | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | **7** | 8 |
| **3**     | 4 | 5 | 6 | **7** | 8 | 9 |
| **4**     | 5 | 6 | **7** | 8 | 9 | 10 |
| **5**     | 6 | **7** | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11 |
| **6**     | **7** | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11 | 12 |

: The sum of two dice. Rows give the first die and columns the second; the six ways to roll a 7 are in bold. {#tbl-dice-sums}

Six of the 36 cells give a sum of 7, so
$P(\text{sum is 7}) = 6/36 = 1/6 \approx 0.167$. Only one cell gives a sum
of 2, so $P(\text{sum is 2}) = 1/36 \approx 0.028$.

**Relative frequency.** Often outcomes are *not* equally likely, and you can't
count your way to an answer. What is the probability that a thumbtack lands
point up? There is no formula; you have to toss it many times and see. The
**relative frequency** of an event is the proportion of trials on which it
happened:
$$
P(A) \approx \frac{\text{number of times } A \text{ happened}}{\text{number of trials}}.
$$

**Subjective probability.** Sometimes you can neither count nor repeat. A
forecaster's "70% chance of rain tomorrow" or a doctor's estimate of a
treatment's success are judgments informed by experience. This book won't
use subjective probabilities, but you should recognize them when you see
them.

### The law of large numbers

Why should the relative frequency approximate a probability at all? Imagine
flipping a fair coin over and over, keeping track of the proportion of
flips that land heads. Here are the first ten flips of one such sequence,
produced by a computer:

```{r}
#| label: coin-flips
#| echo: false
set.seed(113)
flips <- sample(c("H", "T"), size = 10000, replace = TRUE)
ten <- flips[1:10]
```

$$
\text{`r paste(ten, collapse = " ")`}
$$

That is `r sum(ten == "H")` heads in ten flips, a relative frequency of
`r mean(ten == "H")` rather than 0.5. With only a few flips, the relative
frequency often misses 0.5 by quite a bit. @tbl-coin shows what happens as
the same sequence continues.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coin
#| tbl-cap: "The proportion of heads after more and more flips of a fair coin."
#| echo: false
n <- c(10, 100, 1000, 10000)
heads <- sapply(n, function(k) sum(flips[1:k] == "H"))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(n, heads, heads / n),
  col.names = c("Number of flips", "Number of heads", "Proportion of heads"),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  digits = 4
)
```

As the number of flips grows, the proportion of heads tends to settle
closer to 0.5. It doesn't move steadily toward 0.5: between 1,000 and
10,000 flips it actually drifted slightly farther away. But the swings get
smaller as the flips pile up. @fig-lln follows three different sequences, flip by flip.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lln
#| fig-cap: "The running proportion of heads in three separate sequences of 2,000 flips of a fair coin. Each sequence wanders early on, but all settle near 0.5."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2026)
n <- 2000
runs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(i) {
  heads <- sample(c(1, 0), size = n, replace = TRUE)
  data.frame(flip = 1:n, prop = cumsum(heads) / (1:n), run = factor(i))
}))
ggplot(runs, aes(x = flip, y = prop, colour = run)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Number of flips (log scale)", y = "Proportion of heads") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

This pattern is the **law of large numbers**: as a
random process is repeated more and more times, the relative frequency of an
event tends to get closer to its probability. It is the reason a
probability can be read as a *long-run* relative frequency. "The probability
of heads is 0.5" means that in a very long run of flips, about half will be
heads.

::: {.callout-important}
## The law of large numbers is about the long run
The law says nothing about the *next* flip. After five heads in a row, a fair
coin is no more likely to land tails; coins don't remember. Believing that a
run of one outcome makes the other "due" is called the **gambler's fallacy**.
The relative frequency settles down not because the coin evens things out,
but because a few early streaks are swamped by thousands of later flips.
:::

### Rare events

A probability close to 0 describes an event that rarely happens. A common
convention in statistics is to call an event **unusual** if its
probability is 0.05 or less. The cutoff 0.05 is a choice, not a law of
nature; you'll meet other cutoffs later in the book.^[The 0.05 cutoff goes
back to the statistician R. A. Fisher, who in 1925 described it as a
"convenient" limit for judging whether a result should be considered
significant [@fisher1925]. Its wide use since then is largely a matter of
tradition.] This leads to the reasoning behind much of
statistical inference, the **rare event rule**: if, under some assumption,
what you observed would be very unusual, you have reason to doubt the
assumption. If a coin you were told is fair lands heads 20 times in a row,
an event with probability $(1/2)^{20}$, or about 1 in a million, you should
suspect the coin rather than marvel at your luck. You will
return to this idea in @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## Complements and the addition rule

### Complements

The **complement** of an event $A$, written $A^c$, is the event that $A$
does *not* happen. Since either $A$ happens or it doesn't,
$$
P(A^c) = 1 - P(A).
$$ {#eq-complement}
If the probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3, the probability of no rain is
0.7. That looks too simple to be useful, but the **complement rule** often
turns a hard problem into an easy one, as you will see later in this
chapter.

### "Or" and disjoint events

The event "$A$ or $B$" happens when $A$ happens, $B$ happens, or both do.
(In statistics, "or" always includes "both".) Two events are **disjoint**
(also called **mutually exclusive**) if they can't happen at the same time.
When you roll a die, "roll a 1" and "roll a 6" are disjoint; "roll an even
number" and "roll a number greater than 3" are not, since a 4 or a 6 does
both.

For disjoint events, probabilities simply add:
$$
P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) \quad \text{when } A \text{ and } B \text{ are disjoint.}
$$
For example, $P(\text{roll a 1 or a 6}) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3$.

### The general addition rule

When $A$ and $B$ can happen together, adding their probabilities counts the
outcomes in *both* events twice, as the **Venn diagram** in @fig-venn shows.
The fix is to subtract them once:

```{r}
#| label: fig-venn
#| fig-cap: "A Venn diagram. The rectangle is the sample space, and each circle is an event. Outcomes in the overlap belong to both $A$ and $B$, so adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ counts them twice."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
circle <- function(x0, label, r = 1, n = 200) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
  data.frame(x = x0 + r * cos(t), y = r * sin(t), event = label)
}
circles <- rbind(circle(-0.6, "A"), circle(0.6, "B"))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -2.1, xmax = 2.1, ymin = -1.4, ymax = 1.4,
           fill = NA, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_polygon(data = circles, aes(x, y, group = event, fill = event),
               alpha = 0.35, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = c(-1.15, 1.15), y = 0, label = c("A", "B"), size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "A and B\n(counted\ntwice)", size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "steelblue", B = "darkorange")) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

$$
P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B).
$$ {#eq-addition}
This **general addition rule** works for any two events. For disjoint
events, $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0$ and it reduces to the simpler rule above.

**Example.** Roll one die. Let $A$ be "even" $= \{2, 4, 6\}$ and $B$ be
"greater than 3" $= \{4, 5, 6\}$. Both happen for $\{4, 6\}$. By
@eq-addition,
$$
P(A \text{ or } B) = \frac{3}{6} + \frac{3}{6} - \frac{2}{6} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}.
$$
You can check this directly: $A$ or $B$ is $\{2, 4, 5, 6\}$, which has 4 of
the 6 outcomes.

## Two-way tables and conditional probability

### Probabilities from a two-way table

When individuals are classified by two categorical variables, the counts are
arranged in a **two-way table** (also called a **contingency table**).
@tbl-titanic classifies the 2,201 people aboard the *Titanic* on its 1912
voyage, passengers and crew, by sex and by whether they survived. The counts
come from the British Board of Trade's inquiry into the sinking
[@dawson1995].^[Historical sources don't agree exactly on how many people
were aboard, rescued, or lost, so other books may give slightly different
counts.]

```{r}
#| label: tbl-titanic
#| tbl-cap: "People aboard the *Titanic*, by sex and survival."
#| echo: false
titanic <- margin.table(Titanic, c("Sex", "Survived"))
titanic_table <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  tab <- as.data.frame.matrix(x)
  names(tab) <- c("Did not survive", "Survived", if (ncol(tab) == 3) "Total")
  rownames(tab)[rownames(tab) == "Sum"] <- "Total"
  knitr::kable(tab, digits = digits, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
}
titanic_table(addmargins(titanic))
```

The *Total* row and column are the **marginal totals**. If you choose one
person at random from everyone aboard, each of the 2,201 people is equally
likely, so probabilities come straight from counting, as in
@eq-classical:

- $P(\text{survived}) = 711 / 2201 \approx 0.323$
- $P(\text{female}) = 470 / 2201 \approx 0.214$
- $P(\text{female and survived}) = 344 / 2201 \approx 0.156$

A probability that two events both happen, such as
$P(\text{female and survived})$, is called a **joint probability**.

The addition rule gives the probability of choosing someone who was female
or survived (or both):
$$
P(\text{female or survived}) = \frac{470 + 711 - 344}{2201} = \frac{837}{2201} \approx 0.380.
$$
Dividing every count in @tbl-titanic by the grand total of 2,201 turns it
into a table of probabilities, @tbl-titanic-prop. Each entry is the
probability that a randomly chosen person falls in that row and column.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-titanic-prop
#| tbl-cap: "Each count in @tbl-titanic divided by 2,201."
#| echo: false
titanic_table(addmargins(prop.table(titanic)), digits = 3)
```

### Conditional probability

Suppose you are told that the person chosen was female. That changes the
question: now you are choosing from just the 470 women, of whom 344
survived. The probability of survival *given* that the person was female is
$344/470 \approx 0.732$, far higher than the overall 0.323.

The **conditional probability** of $B$ given $A$, written $P(B \mid A)$, is
the probability that $B$ happens when you already know that $A$ has
happened. Knowing $A$ shrinks the sample space to the outcomes in $A$, which
gives the formula
$$
P(B \mid A) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)}.
$$ {#eq-conditional}
With the *Titanic* numbers,
$$
P(\text{survived} \mid \text{female}) = \frac{344/2201}{470/2201} = \frac{344}{470} \approx 0.732.
$$
In a two-way table you don't need the formula: restrict attention to the row
(or column) for what you know, and divide by that row's total. Doing this
for each row of @tbl-titanic gives @tbl-titanic-rows.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-titanic-rows
#| tbl-cap: "Each row of @tbl-titanic divided by its row total: survival given sex."
#| echo: false
titanic_table(prop.table(titanic, 1), digits = 3)
```

About 73% of women survived, compared with about 21% of men
(@fig-titanic-survival). The difference has a historical explanation: the
lifeboats were loaded under the order "women and children first."

```{r}
#| label: fig-titanic-survival
#| fig-cap: "The percentage of people aboard the *Titanic* who survived, among females and among males. Each bar is a conditional probability."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
surv <- as.data.frame(prop.table(titanic, 1))
surv <- surv[surv$Survived == "Yes", ]
ggplot(surv, aes(x = Sex, y = Freq)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(Freq, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Percent who survived") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Order matters
$P(B \mid A)$ and $P(A \mid B)$ are different questions.
$P(\text{survived} \mid \text{female}) \approx 0.732$, but
$P(\text{female} \mid \text{survived}) = 344/711 \approx 0.484$: among
survivors, slightly fewer than half were women. Mixing the two up is
called **confusion of the inverse**. It is one of the most common errors in
reasoning about probability, from courtrooms to medical test results; you'll
see a striking medical example in @sec-bayes.
:::

## Independence and the multiplication rule

### Independent events

Two events are **independent** if knowing that one happened doesn't change
the probability of the other:
$$
P(B \mid A) = P(B).
$$
Successive flips of a coin are independent; the coin has no memory. Sex and
survival on the *Titanic* are **dependent**: learning that a passenger was
female raised the probability of survival from 0.323 to 0.732.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Disjoint is not the same as independent
*Disjoint* means two events can't happen together. *Independent* means
knowing one happened doesn't change the probability of the other. The two
ideas are easy to confuse, but they are different.

- **Disjoint, so not independent.** Roll one die. "Roll a 1" and "roll a 6"
  are disjoint. Before the roll, $P(\text{6}) = 1/6$. But if you learn that
  the roll was a 1, a 6 has become impossible:
  $P(\text{6} \mid \text{1}) = 0$. Learning one event changed the
  probability of the other, so they are dependent.
- **Independent, so not disjoint.** Flip a coin twice. "Heads on the first
  flip" and "heads on the second flip" are independent, since the coin has
  no memory. They are not disjoint: both happen whenever you flip HH.

In fact, two disjoint events (each with probability greater than 0) are
*always* dependent, because learning that one happened rules the other out.
:::

### The multiplication rule

Rearranging @eq-conditional gives a rule for the probability that two
events *both* happen. The **multiplication rule** is
$$
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A).
$$ {#eq-multiplication}
When $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$, and this becomes
$$
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \quad \text{when } A \text{ and } B \text{ are independent.}
$$
The same idea extends to more than two independent events: multiply all
their probabilities.

This gives a second way to check for independence: see whether
$P(A \text{ and } B)$ equals $P(A) \cdot P(B)$. For the *Titanic*,
$$
P(\text{female}) \cdot P(\text{survived}) \approx 0.214 \times 0.323 \approx 0.069,
$$
but the actual joint probability is $P(\text{female and survived}) \approx 0.156$,
more than twice as large. Sex and survival are not independent, which
agrees with what conditional probabilities showed.

**Example (independent).** Roll two fair dice. The dice don't affect each
other, so the two rolls are independent, and the probability of rolling two
sixes is $\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}$. This agrees with
@tbl-dice-sums, where only one of the 36 cells is a pair of sixes.

::: {.callout-note}
## A standard deck of cards
Several examples and exercises use a standard deck of 52 playing cards. The
deck has four **suits** of 13 cards each: hearts and diamonds (red), clubs
and spades (black). Each suit has an ace, the numbers 2 through 10, and three
**face cards**: a jack, a queen, and a king. So the deck has 4 aces, 12 face
cards, and 26 red cards. A shuffled deck makes every card equally likely to
be drawn.
:::

**Example (dependent).** Draw two cards from a shuffled 52-card deck without
putting the first back. The probability that both are aces is
$$
P(\text{first ace}) \cdot P(\text{second ace} \mid \text{first ace}) = \frac{4}{52} \cdot \frac{3}{51} \approx 0.0045.
$$
The second factor is $3/51$, not $4/52$, because one ace and one card are
already gone. Drawing **without replacement** makes the draws dependent.
If instead the first card were put back and the deck reshuffled, drawing
**with replacement**, the draws would be independent, and the probability
would be $\frac{4}{52} \cdot \frac{4}{52} \approx 0.0059$.

::: {.callout-note}
## The 5% guideline
When you sample without replacement from a large population, removing a few
individuals barely changes the proportions that remain. If your sample is no
more than 5% of the population, you can treat the selections as independent.
This guideline will matter in @sec-discrete-rv.
:::

### "At least one": the complement rule at work

In the 1600s, gamblers bet on rolling at least one six in four rolls of a
die.^[Questions about this bet and others like it were raised by the French
writer and gambler Antoine Gombaud, the Chevalier de Méré. They prompted a
famous exchange of letters in 1654 between the mathematicians Blaise Pascal
and Pierre de Fermat, often taken as the beginning of probability theory.
An exercise at the end of this chapter looks at a second bet de Méré made.] Listing every way to get "at least one" six is tedious, but its
complement, "no sixes at all", is easy. The four rolls are independent, and
each misses a six with probability $5/6$, so
$$
P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - P(\text{no sixes}) = 1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4 \approx 0.518.
$$

```{r}
#| label: at-least-one-sim
#| echo: false
set.seed(1654)
got_six <- replicate(10000, any(sample(1:6, size = 4, replace = TRUE) == 6))
```

A computer simulation agrees. In 10,000 simulated sets of four rolls, at
least one six appeared in `r format(sum(got_six), big.mark = ",")` of them,
a relative frequency of `r mean(got_six)`. The gamblers who took this bet
won slightly more often than they lost.

## Bayes' rule {#sec-bayes}

### A surprising test result

Medical screening tests are not perfect. A **false positive** is a positive
result for someone who doesn't have the condition; a **false negative** is a
negative result for someone who does. Consider a hypothetical screening test
for a disease that affects 1% of a population. The proportion of a
population that has a disease is called its **prevalence**, so here the
prevalence is 1%.

- The test is positive for 95% of people who *have* the disease. This is
  the test's **sensitivity**.
- The test is negative for 95% of people who *don't* have it. This is the
  test's **specificity**. It gives a false positive for the other 5%.

Your test comes back positive. What is the probability that you have the
disease? Many people guess something close to 95%. The true answer is much
smaller.

### Thinking in counts

The easiest way to see why is to imagine testing 10,000 people and building
a two-way table, just as you did with the *Titanic* data.

- 1% of 10,000, or 100 people, have the disease. The test catches 95% of
  them, so 95 test positive and 5 test negative.
- The other 9,900 don't have the disease. The test wrongly flags 5% of them,
  so 495 test positive and 9,405 test negative.

|              | Positive | Negative |  Total |
|--------------|---------:|---------:|-------:|
| Disease      |       95 |        5 |    100 |
| No disease   |      495 |    9,405 |  9,900 |
| Total        |      590 |    9,410 | 10,000 |

: Expected results of testing 10,000 people {#tbl-screening}

Now read the answer from the *Positive* column of @tbl-screening. Of the 590
people who test positive, only 95 have the disease:
$$
P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive}) = \frac{95}{590} \approx 0.161.
$$
A positive result raises the probability that you have the disease from 1%
to about 16%, but most positive results are false positives. That's because
the disease is rare: 5% of a very large healthy group (495 people)
outnumbers 95% of a small sick group (95 people).

### Tree diagrams

A **tree diagram** shows the same reasoning as a sequence of branches. The
first set of branches splits the population by disease status, and the
second by test result. Following a path from left to right and multiplying
the probabilities along it is the multiplication rule, @eq-multiplication.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tree
#| fig-cap: "A tree diagram for the screening test. Probabilities on the second set of branches are conditional on the first. The probability at the end of each path is the product of the probabilities along it."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
nodes <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2),
  y = c(0.75, 0.25, 0.9, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1),
  label = c("Disease", "No disease",
            "Positive\n0.01 × 0.95 = 0.0095", "Negative\n0.01 × 0.05 = 0.0005",
            "Positive\n0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0495", "Negative\n0.99 × 0.95 = 0.9405")
)
edges <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1), y = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25, 0.25),
  xend = nodes$x, yend = nodes$y,
  prob = c("0.01", "0.99", "0.95", "0.05", "0.05", "0.95")
)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "grey50") +
  geom_label(data = edges, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = (y + yend) / 2, label = prob),
             size = 3.5, label.size = 0, fill = "white") +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
             hjust = c(0.5, 0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0), size = 3.5, fill = "grey95") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2.8), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.08)) +
  theme_void()
```

In @fig-tree, two paths end in a positive test, with probabilities 0.0095
and 0.0495. The probability of having the disease given a positive test is
the share of the first path:
$$
P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive}) = \frac{0.0095}{0.0095 + 0.0495} = \frac{0.0095}{0.059} \approx 0.161,
$$
the same answer as the table.

### The formula

Writing that calculation with letters gives **Bayes' rule**.^[It is named
for Thomas Bayes, an English minister. His essay on the subject was
published in 1763, after his death, by his friend Richard Price.] If $A$ is an
event (having the disease) and $B$ is something you observe (a positive
test), then
$$
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)}{P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A) + P(A^c) \cdot P(B \mid A^c)}.
$$ {#eq-bayes}
The numerator is the probability of the path through $A$ and $B$. The
denominator adds the probabilities of *every* path that ends in $B$. In
words, Bayes' rule turns $P(B \mid A)$, which is what the test's makers can
measure, into $P(A \mid B)$, which is what a patient wants to know. It is
how you avoid confusion of the inverse, the error described in "Order
matters."

The probability $P(A)$ that you start with is called the **prior
probability**, and the updated probability $P(A \mid B)$ is the **posterior
probability**. The prior makes a big difference. @tbl-prior applies
@eq-bayes to the same test, used on populations where the disease is more
or less common.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior
#| tbl-cap: "The probability of disease after a positive test, for the same test used where the disease is more or less common."
#| echo: false
prior <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.10, 0.50)
posterior <- prior * 0.95 / (prior * 0.95 + (1 - prior) * 0.05)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(prior, round(posterior, 3)),
  col.names = c("Prior: P(disease)", "Posterior: P(disease | positive)")
)
```

The same positive result means about a 2% chance of disease when the
disease is very rare, and a 95% chance when half the people tested have it.
This is why doctors often use screening tests only on people already at
higher risk, and confirm a positive result with a second test.

### Updating with a second test

Bayes' rule describes how a probability should be *updated* as evidence
comes in, and each update can feed the next. Suppose your first test is
positive, so your probability of having the disease is now 0.161. You take
a second, independent test with the same sensitivity and specificity, and
it is also positive. The posterior from the first test becomes the prior
for the second:
$$
P(\text{disease} \mid \text{two positives}) = \frac{0.161 \times 0.95}{0.161 \times 0.95 + 0.839 \times 0.05} = \frac{0.153}{0.153 + 0.042} \approx 0.785.
$$
One positive result raised the probability from 1% to about 16%; a second
raises it to about 79%. (This assumes the two tests make their mistakes
independently. A test that errs for some reason particular to you, such as
something in your blood that confuses it, may make the same mistake twice.)

## Counting methods (optional) {#sec-counting}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
This section is optional. If you skip it, the only tool you'll need later
is your calculator's nCr key, which the binomial distribution in
@sec-discrete-rv uses.
:::

Using @eq-classical requires counting outcomes, and sample spaces can be
very large. Three counting tools cover most situations.

**The fundamental counting rule.** If a first choice can be made in $m$
ways, and for each of those there are $n$ ways to make a second choice, the
two can be made together in $m \cdot n$ ways. A password of two capital
letters followed by three digits can be formed in $26 \cdot 26 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 = 676{,}000$ ways.

**Factorials.** The number of ways to arrange $n$ different items in order is
$n! = n \cdot (n - 1) \cdots 2 \cdot 1$, read "$n$ **factorial**." Five books
can be lined up on a shelf in $5! = 120$ ways. By convention, $0! = 1$.^[This
convention makes the formulas below work in every case. For example, there
is exactly one way to choose all $n$ of $n$ items, and indeed
${}_nC_n = \dfrac{n!}{n!\,0!} = 1$ only if $0! = 1$.]

**Permutations and combinations.** When you choose $r$ items from $n$
different items, the count depends on whether the order of selection
matters. A **permutation** is an ordered selection; a **combination** is an
unordered one.

- Choosing a president, vice president, and secretary from a club of 30
  members is a permutation, since the roles differ:
  $30 \cdot 29 \cdot 28 = 24{,}360$ ways. In general,
  ${}_nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$.
- Choosing a 3-person committee from the same 30 members is a combination.
  Each committee can be ordered in $3! = 6$ ways, so there are
  $24{,}360 / 6 = 4{,}060$ committees. In general,
  ${}_nC_r = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$.

Most calculators have keys for these, often labeled $n!$, nPr, and
nCr.

**Example: a lottery.** In a lottery where you pick 6 numbers from 1 to 49
and win only by matching all 6 numbers drawn, order doesn't matter, so the
number of possible tickets is
$$
{}_{49}C_6 = \frac{49!}{6!\,43!} = \frac{49 \cdot 48 \cdot 47 \cdot 46 \cdot 45 \cdot 44}{6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = 13{,}983{,}816.
$$

Each ticket is equally likely, so the probability of winning with one ticket
is $1/13{,}983{,}816$: about 1 chance in 14 million.

## Exercises

### Basic ideas of probability

1. Which of the following cannot be probabilities? Explain.
   $\quad 0 \qquad 1.2 \qquad -0.1 \qquad 3/5 \qquad 5/3 \qquad 1 \qquad 0.001$

2. A coin is flipped three times.
   a. List the sample space. (There are 8 equally likely outcomes, such as
      HHT.)
   b. Find the probability of exactly two heads.
   c. Find the probability of at least one head. Which rule gives the
      quickest answer?

3. Two fair dice are rolled. Use @tbl-dice-sums to find:
   a. $P(\text{sum is 11})$
   b. $P(\text{doubles})$, the probability that both dice show the same
      number
   c. $P(\text{sum is 10 or more})$

4. A student says, "I've lost the last five games of chance I played, so I'm
   due for a win." Explain what is wrong with this reasoning.

5. For each event, decide whether it is *unusual* in the sense of this
   chapter.
   a. An event with probability 0.03.
   b. An event with probability 0.20.
   c. Getting 10 heads in 10 flips of a fair coin, which has probability
      $(1/2)^{10}$.

### Complements and the addition rule

6. A spinner is divided into four regions. The probabilities of landing in
   regions A, B, and C are 0.25, 0.4, and 0.15. What is the probability of
   landing in region D? Which rule did you use?

7. One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck.
   a. Find the probability that it is a heart or a face card (jack, queen,
      or king).
   b. Are the events "heart" and "face card" disjoint? Explain.
   c. Find the probability that it is *not* a face card.

### Two-way tables and conditional probability

8. Use the *Titanic* table of sex and survival in this chapter to find:
   a. $P(\text{male})$
   b. $P(\text{did not survive} \mid \text{male})$
   c. $P(\text{male} \mid \text{did not survive})$

   Explain in words why your answers to (b) and (c) differ.

9. The table below classifies the 2,201 people aboard the *Titanic* by
   class (for passengers) or as crew, and by survival. One person is chosen
   at random.

   | Class  | Did not survive | Survived | Total |
   |--------|----------------:|---------:|------:|
   | First  |             122 |      203 |   325 |
   | Second |             167 |      118 |   285 |
   | Third  |             528 |      178 |   706 |
   | Crew   |             673 |      212 |   885 |
   | Total  |           1,490 |      711 | 2,201 |

   a. Find $P(\text{survived} \mid \text{first class})$ and
      $P(\text{survived} \mid \text{third class})$.
   b. Find $P(\text{first class} \mid \text{survived})$.
   c. Find $P(\text{crew or survived})$.
   d. Are class and survival independent? Use your answers to (a) to
      explain.
   e. Check your answer to (d) a second way: compare
      $P(\text{first class and survived})$ with
      $P(\text{first class}) \cdot P(\text{survived})$.

### Independence and the multiplication rule

10. Can two disjoint events, each with probability greater than 0, be
    independent? Explain, and illustrate your answer with an example of
    your own.

11. Two cards are drawn from a standard deck. Find the probability that both
    are hearts (a) if the first card is replaced and the deck reshuffled
    before the second draw, and (b) if it is not.

12. A quality inspector selects 3 items from a shipment of 10,000, of which
    2% are defective. Explain why the selections can be treated as
    independent, and find the probability that none of the 3 is defective.

13. A home has three smoke detectors that work independently. Each one
    detects a fire with probability 0.9. Find the probability that at least
    one of them detects a fire. Why is it easier to begin with the
    complement?

14. The Chevalier de Méré also bet that in 24 rolls of a *pair* of dice, at
    least one roll would be a double six.
    a. What is the probability of a double six on one roll of a pair of
       dice?
    b. Use the complement rule to find the probability of at least one
       double six in 24 rolls.
    c. Was this a good bet for de Méré? Compare your answer with the bet on
       one die in this chapter.

### Bayes' rule

15. A company tests its employees for drug use. Suppose 4% of employees use
    the drug. The test has sensitivity 98% and specificity 97%.
    a. What percentage of non-users get a false positive?
    b. Imagine 10,000 employees. Make a two-way table of drug use and test
       result, like @tbl-screening.
    c. Find the probability that an employee who tests positive is a user.
       Check your answer with Bayes' rule, @eq-bayes.
    d. An employee who tests positive takes a second, independent test,
       which is also positive. Use your answer to (c) as the new prior, and
       find the probability that the employee is a user.

16. Explain, without calculating, why a positive result on the screening
    test in this chapter would be more convincing if the disease affected
    20% of the population instead of 1%.

### Counting methods (optional)

17. A class of 25 students must choose 4 students to present a project.
    a. How many different groups of 4 are possible?
    b. How many ways are there to choose a first, second, third, and fourth
       presenter?
    c. Explain why your answer to (b) is $4! = 24$ times your answer
       to (a).

18. A bank card uses a 4-digit PIN, and any digits 0 through 9 may be used
    in each position, including repeats.
    a. How many different PINs are possible?
    b. A thief who doesn't know your PIN guesses one at random. What is the
       probability of guessing correctly?
    c. The card is blocked after 3 wrong attempts. If the thief tries 3
       different PINs, what is the probability that one of them is right?
